title: A Strange But Elegant Approach to a Surprisingly Hard Problem (GJK Algorithm)
beats: Do two shapes intersect? Easy to see, hard for computers across circles, polygons, odd shapes
Promise: roller coaster of shifts in perspective, not a straight line
Convex vs concave; split concave into convex pieces (nine triangles)
Thought experiment: infinite point sets and a magic computer; intersection means a common point
Common point iff difference of points is origin; Minkowski sum/difference defined
Two properties: difference of convex is convex; intersection means origin inside
Full difference is infeasible; sample three points and get a triangle around origin
Simplex as triangle in 2D, tetrahedron in 3D
Need a scheme to choose points: detour to furthest point in a direction
Support function; support of Minkowski difference = difference of support points
Support via dot product; polygon max over vertices, circle radius times direction; shape-agnostic
Bird's-eye run: direction, support point, toward origin, sanity check, normal direction; intersecting then non-intersecting case
Pat on back; list the five open questions to answer one by one
Past-origin check is dot product with d; perpendicular via vector triple product
Voronoi regions; ask how many of the seven regions need checking
Eliminate five regions by reasoning about how point a was found; only two checks remain
Full implementation, line case and triangle case
Three shifts of perspective: infinite points, Minkowski difference, support functions
Original paper dense; tip hat; sign off

theory: The video frames the algorithm as a sequence of reframings of the problem, each of which makes it easier, and teaches the high-level loop before the proofs of each step. Open questions are enumerated explicitly so the later detail has places to land.

Scene builder: keep same two shapes across all scenes, color-code the Minkowski difference

Evals: check that a recap lists the reframings in order
